summary:
I built the Crew Health Monitor, a web-based dashboard that tracks the health of a four-person astronaut crew on a deep-space mission. It shows live heart rate, blood oxygen, core temperature, breathing rate and blood pressure for each astronaut, along with cabin CO₂, radiation dose rate and cumulative radiation exposure. It runs on simulated data.

It addresses the challenge in three ways. Thresholds adjust to each activity, so a high heart rate during exercise or a spacewalk doesn’t cause a false alarm. Each astronaut has a personal baseline, so the system flags a slow drift, such as a rising resting heart rate, before any fixed limit is crossed. Every alert is logged with a timestamp and a suggested action. Simulation buttons let users trigger a solar particle event, a CO₂ scrubber fault or an illness.

This matters because crews on long missions can’t get quick medical help from Earth, so problems need to be caught early and handled onboard. This version is a demonstration, not a medical device, and a real system would need clinical review and certification.
details:
The Crew Health Monitor is a single-page web dashboard for a four-person crew on a deep-space mission. A simulator produces a new set of readings every second for each astronaut: heart rate, blood oxygen, core temperature, breathing rate and blood pressure. It also simulates cabin CO₂ and radiation dose rate, and tracks each person’s cumulative radiation dose. Each astronaut has a card showing their vitals, a heart-rate trend line and an overall status of Normal, Watch or Alert. An alert engine compares every reading against limits that change with the astronaut’s activity (rest, sleep, exercise or spacewalk). It also compares each person’s resting heart rate with their own baseline and logs a Watch alert when it drifts upward, even if no fixed limit has been crossed. Each log entry has a timestamp and a suggested action. Buttons let a user trigger a solar particle event, a CO₂ scrubber fault or an illness, and change an astronaut’s activity.

Benefits and intended impact

On long missions, help from Earth can be delayed, so the crew has to spot health problems early and act on them onboard. The project aims to cut false alarms, catch slow changes that fixed limits miss, and tell the crew what to do next. It also works as a training and prototyping tool for how such a system could behave.

Tools used

HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with SVG for the trend lines and Google Fonts for typography. I built it with Claude and published it as a hosted web page. There is no hardware, and all data is simulated.

Creativity

The creative parts are the personal baselines, activity-aware thresholds, and the single environment where heart rate, radiation and CO₂ interact. CO₂ rises affect crew breathing, and a spacewalk increases radiation exposure.

Factors considered

  • Safety: status uses symbols and text as well as color.
  • Usability: large readable numbers and keyboard access.
  • Accessibility: light and dark themes, and a layout that works on phones and desktops.
  • Limits: the thresholds are illustrative rather than clinical, and it is not a medical device.
